items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Our first Cosmos-H-Dreams release, built on Cosmos-Predict2.5, brought interactive generative simulation to dVRK tabletop suturing, a foundational proving ground for surgical robotics. As world foundation model (WFM), Cosmos-H-Dreams demonstrated an alternative to numerical simulation: rather than explicitly modeling scene geometry, tissue deformation, and physical interactions, it learned visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics, yielding interactive tabletop task simulation with high realism. Today, Cosmos3-H-Dreams advances this capability by learning from video and robot kinematics recording during clinical procedures on the CMR Surgical Versius platform. To our knowledge, this is the first real-time generative surgical simulator trained on clinical cholecystectomy recordings to support live kinematic control. Powered by Cosmos 3 and accelerated with FlashDreams, NVIDIA’s accelerated streaming-inference library, Cosmos3-H-Dreams runs interactively on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. In a controlled tabletop environment like that of Cosmos-H-Dreams, instruments operate against a relatively simple background. Inside the human body, however, small instrument movements can affect an entire scene: tissue stretches under traction, reflections shift, structures become occluded, and smoke changes visibility. Given an initial image and supplied tool actions, a generative simulator must capture these responses while preserving the anatomy and instruments as it generates each new block of video. Small errors can accumulate over time, gradually changing instrument geometry or anatomical structure, making temporal consistency essential. Visual realism is therefore a starting point for validation, not proof of biomechanical accuracy. The generated scene must also follow the controls: translation, rotation, and gripper commands should produce coherent anatomical consequences. A plausible-looking rollout that ignores those commands cannot serve as an interactive environment. Maintaining this fidelity and responsiveness in a live control loop requires low latency generation. Cosmos3-H-Dreams addresses this setting through a model specialized for clinical cholecystectomy and distilled for real-time generation, bringing action-conditioned interaction into scenes with complex anatomy, tissue motion, and occlusion. Cosmos3-H-Dreams builds on Cosmos3-H-Embodied-Nano, a 16-billion-parameter model pretrained on Open-H-Embodiment, and specializes a bidirectional teacher on curated cholecystectomy video and kinematics. Sample selection targets two visible, engaged instruments, a left Cadiere grasper and a right monopolar hook, and limits camera commands to emphasize instrument-driven interaction. The model uses 28 action dimensions: pose and gripper information for both arms, plus energy controls, thumbstick axes and thumbstick buttons. Training uses 832 x 480 video with actions aligned at 10 Hz; that sampling rate is distinct from runtime generation throughput. Cosmos3-H-Dreams combines a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long autoregressive rollouts with accelerated streaming inference through FlashDreams. We first adapt the bidirectional teacher on 24 future frames, then extend the horizon to 72 frames, 2.4 and 7.2 seconds at 10 Hz. This gives the teacher longer sequences over which to learn surgical dynamics. Next, distillation turns the bidirectional teacher into a causal student that can generate video in short blocks as new actions arrive. Causal teacher forcing prepares the student for sequential generation using recorded context. Self-Forcing then trains it on its own generated context, guided by the teacher and a learned critic. This helps address the accumulation of errors during interactive rollouts. The first released student uses four denoising steps per generated block. We then train that student further with a two-step schedule to produce the second release checkpoint. The two-step model is separately trained, not simply the four-step model run with fewer sampling steps. Fewer denoising steps results in faster inference time at the expense of lower visual quality. Both checkpoints let developers explore the balance between visual quality and inference cost. FlashDreams supplies the accelerated streaming runtime. Long rollouts also require managing the model’s attention history. The Cosmos3-H-Dreams integration uses an adapted FadeMem module that consolidates the growing key/value cache during long rollouts. This complements Self-Forcing: distillation addresses how the model learns from its generated history, while cache consolidation addresses how that history is stored during streaming generation. During a clinical procedure there may be complications or some room for the surgeon to perform “novel” movements. Therefore, a simulator must be able to generalize beyond the training data, and produce coherent frames with unseen movements. The demonstrations below show Cosmos3-H-Dreams generating different cholecystectomy scenes conditioned on instrument actions recorded with a VR headset. The two videos begin with the same initial frame but follow different action sequences illustrating how instrument control leads to distinct continuations of the same scene with physically accurate tissue deformations. Furthermore, these rollouts allow us to inspect whether instruments follow the controls, whether tissue responds coherently to interaction, and whether anatomical and instrument appearance remain consistent over time. Cosmos3-H-Dreams includes four-step and two-step checkpoints for cholecystectomy. The system can be adapted to other datasets and embodiments with synchronized video and compatible action representations. To train a real-time student model on your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and Self-Forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide. It describes data preparation, public teacher-training tools, and the distillation stages. Controller integrations must use the same action conventions and normalization as training. The advance in visual realism opens several research directions: - Model the full procedure. Expand coverage and temporal consistency so all phases of cholecystectomy can be explored systematically, with clear task boundaries and success criteria. - Connect generative and numerical simulation. Combine learned visual realism with explicit geometry, contact and tissue mechanics. Numerical models and measured data could help constrain and validate deformation, making simulation behavior inspectable as well as convincing. - Evaluate with surgeons. Assess anatomical accuracy, instrument behavior and tissue response, turning expert feedback into reproducible benchmarks. - Support more instruments. items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Franchisee reconciles cash in 94% less time with ChatGPT Work An independent Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon franchisee cut repricing time by 95% and built a workflow that could free up $100K in cash flow. 95% Reduction in time required for pricing analysis, from 5 days to 1 to 2 hours $100K Maximum annual cash flow that could be freed up with optimized labor workflow 4 Hours of manual work saved every payroll 94% Reduction in time spent on monthly cash reconciliation Ted Taylor entered the restaurant business after a 25-year career in the semiconductor industry. Today, he’s an independent franchisee operating three co-branded Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon restaurants across New Mexico. Running quick-service restaurants means balancing the customer experience with a lot of work customers never see, like menu pricing, staffing, equipment maintenance, and policies. Ted uses OpenAI technology to get through all of it faster. With ChatGPT, Ted accelerates time-consuming tasks like research and drafting, and he uses ChatGPT Work to gather and analyze volumes of data across pricing, sales, forecasts, schedules, and labor and to get recommendations on where each restaurant needs attention, reducing repricing time by 95% and shaving 4 hours off payroll runs. “ChatGPT Work’s recommendations are so good that it’s much faster to start there and then make adjustments.” Repricing menus is an annual undertaking that requires a complex analysis of recipe costs, item popularity, local competitor pricing, portion sizes, and the different economics of in-store and delivery orders. Ted uses ChatGPT Work to bring those factors together and get pricing recommendations in 1 - 2 hours instead of 5 days. “It used to take me a few days of work to analyze and come up with item-level pricing; whereas, ChatGPT Work tears through it in a matter of moments and does it more thoroughly.” Ted first uses ChatGPT Work to research and establish his pricing targets and pricing strategies based on local competitors’ pricing trends, portion sizes, and relative food quality. He then gives ChatGPT Work a categorized list of menu items with their current in-store and delivery prices. He specifies how much he wants each set of prices to increase overall and which items should receive larger or smaller increases, largely based on the earlier analysis from ChatGPT. He can make the analysis more detailed by adding item-level sales history and supplier prices. ChatGPT Work can use these inputs to estimate sales impacts from price changes and to optimize item-level pricing around cost of goods targets. ChatGPT Work returns a spreadsheet with recommended in-store and delivery prices. It will even relate the pricing changes to an overall pricing strategy designed to optimize business outcomes like customer retention, minimizing price shocks, and best positioning of add-ons. The first time Ted used ChatGPT Work for pricing, he also ran the analysis manually. “ChatGPT Work made a deeper local comparison and helped me avoid increases that would have made some items uncompetitive,” he said. Ted immediately switched to using ChatGPT to develop the first recommendations. Ted uses ChatGPT Work to help manage labor costs in two ways: reviewing how labor is tracking across his three restaurants and testing a better way to build the weekly schedule. For the labor analysis, Ted gave ChatGPT Work read-only access to his sales and labor data. When he runs the analysis, it compares scheduled, budgeted, and actual hours with forecast and actual sales. It also reviews the previous 12 weeks to account for stores that routinely come in above or below their sales forecasts. The resulting report flags overtime, shifts running longer than planned, and gaps in coverage, and highlights what a manager should review. For the scheduling test, Ted gave ChatGPT Work an employee roster with each person’s role, training, availability, and pay, along with the store’s staffing needs at different sales levels. He and the manager compared ChatGPT Work’s proposed schedule with what she would have built, identified missing rules about when to add staff during busy periods, and refined the instructions for ChatGPT Work. ChatGPT Work now produces a full schedule for that location. The manager checks it over, makes adjustments if needed, and enters it into the restaurant’s scheduling system. Ted estimates that better scheduling could eventually reduce hourly labor costs by one to two percentage points of sales across all three restaurants, which could add $50,000 to $100,000 in free cash flow annually that can be utilized for increased pay, bonuses, investment in the business, or increased profit distributions. Ted also uses ChatGPT Work for day-to-day operations, from developing HR policies to reconciling cash and managing supply and repair requests. When New Mexico started requiring restaurants to keep a written procedure for bodily-fluid incidents, Ted used ChatGPT to write a draft in about 30 seconds. When Ted needed a social media policy for his employee handbook, ChatGPT helped him quickly draft guidance that an outside HR firm later reviewed without making any changes. Ted uses ChatGPT Work to reconcile cash monthly across his three restaurants. He uploads each store’s cash transaction data and bank records, and ChatGPT Work compares the transactions with the corresponding deposits. Monthly reconciliation used to take three hours, and now it takes 5-10 minutes. He also cut four hours of manual work from every payroll cycle by using ChatGPT Work to summarize payroll inputs. To help keep restaurants running smoothly, Ted also used ChatGPT Work to build a web portal where employees can request supplies or repairs. The portal notifies him through a dedicated email address and tracks each request’s status. Ted’s approach to using ChatGPT Work is practical for any small-business owner. He gives ChatGPT the same data and guidelines he’d use to make a decision and compares its output with how he’d do the work himself. As he gains confidence in the results, he expands his use to more tasks around the business, always reviewing the results before implementing. For Ted, the value of ChatGPT Work goes beyond hours saved. Now he can do analysis he might otherwise skip and spend more time on customers, employees, and growing the business.

items.extracted_text_for_analysis: OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio(opens in a new window), a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate the complex process of drug development. We’re bringing Orchestra’s team and technology together with Rosalind, our AI models and tools for life sciences research. Our goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work needed to turn them into treatments that reach patients sooner. Developing a new medicine is extraordinarily complex, taking roughly 10 to 15 years on average from target discovery to regulatory approval in the United States. Beyond the science, teams must orchestrate programs across internal departments and external partners, often relying on disconnected systems. We’re now at an inflection point where AI can help take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows. Rosalind brings our AI models and tools to life sciences researchers. GPT‑Rosalind helps scientists reason through questions in biology and chemistry. Rosalind Workbench connects those capabilities with scientific tools and data to help researchers analyze results and plan experiments. Orchestra brings a team with experience across biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development. Together, we aim to build agents that help teams connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine. Orchestra Bio is a platform where people and AI agents work together to advance drug programs. Scientists and program leaders delegate the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, freeing up time to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays. A problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others. A failed manufacturing batch, for example, can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra’s agents help teams identify which activities and timelines are affected, gather the relevant information, and compare ways to respond. Scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next. Realizing the potential of AI in life sciences requires close collaboration with the organizations working at the forefront of drug discovery and development. Our partnership with Novo Nordisk aims to translate its scale and scientific expertise into faster R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance. At Moderna, AI is helping teams translate insights from complex data into experimental workflows, with the potential to accelerate R&D. Our vision is for AI to help scientists across the full process of discovering and developing new medicines: exploring ideas, designing experiments, interpreting results, and coordinating the work needed to advance promising treatments. Bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind is a step toward that vision. Alongside researchers and our partners, we aim to make more discoveries possible and help new medicines reach patients sooner.

items.extracted_excerpt: We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done. TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini. TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale. The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in. Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about. To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers. TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command: pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU. Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it. from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, device_map="tpu", # will load model directly on the TPU ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) inputs = tokenizer("The future of AI is", return_tensors="pt").to("tpu") out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=64) print(tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True)) The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup. TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain. import torch from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium", dtype=torch.bfloat16 ) pipe.to("tpu") # eager mode: that's the whole change # optional: compiled mode pipe.transformer.compile(backend="tpu", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False) image = pipe("a corgi astronaut planting a flag on a pizza moon").images[0] The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph. Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe. Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4: TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1 The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost. TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model: from kernels import get_kernel from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.integrations.moe import ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS repo_id = "tengomucho/ragged-dot-tpu" kernel = get_kernel(repo_id, version=1, trust_remote_code=[repo_id]) ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS.register("tokamax_ragged_dot", kernel.experts_forward) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507", experts_implementation="tokamax_ragged_dot", ) The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B. Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation. We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard]. The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress! It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream. If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do. TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu". We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

items.extracted_text_for_analysis: 2026年10月5日、Sakana AIは昨年に続き2回目となるエンジニア向けOpen Houseを開催しました。昨年はApplied Research Engineerに絞った内容でしたが、今年はApplied Research Engineer / Forward Deployed Engineer / Software Engineer / Solution Engineer / Cybersecurity Engineerの5職種を対象として、各職種で働くメンバーが「何をしているか」「何が面白いか」などを語りました。また、Q&Aセッションには多くの質問が寄せられました。本記事ではイベントの内容をお伝えします。 会社紹介：日本からAI主権をつくる —— David Ha 共同創業者兼CEOであるDavid Haの会社紹介から始まりました。ゴールドマン・サックスのデリバティブ・トレーダーから研究者へ転身し、Googleで「World Models」や「Sketch-RNN」など現代の生成AIの基礎となる研究に携わってきたDavidは、「キャリアチェンジを考えている皆さんと同じで、私もキャリアを変えた一人です」と来場者に語りかけました。 会社紹介を行う共同創業者兼CEOのDavid Ha 社名の「Sakana AI」には、絵本『スイミー』に着想を得た思想が込められています。知性とは一匹の魚ではなく、群れ全体の「集合知」である。他と同じ方向に泳ぐのではなく自分たちの方向を見出し世界に挑む——このアイデンティティがSakana AIの根底にあります。 Davidが見据えるのは「日本から世界と戦えるAI企業をつくること」です。海外製のオープンソースモデルには開発国の政治的・文化的バイアスが含まれ、日本の政治や文化に関する質問に誤答したり回答を拒否したりする課題があります。 そこでSakana AIは事前学習（Pre-training）、事後学習（Post-training）、オーケストレーション（Orchestration）の3層で「AI主権」の確立を進めています。事前学習では日本独自のエージェント・ネイティブLLMをスクラッチから開発し、事後学習ではSakana AIが開発した「Namazu」によって海外モデルを日本の文化・習慣に適応させ、オーケストレーションでは地政学リスク等で海外モデルが使えなくなる事態に備え、複数モデルを賢く切り替える「Fugu」を展開しています。 直近半年でSakana Chat, Sakana Marlin, Sakana Fugu, Sakana Translateとプロダクトポートフォリオを一気に拡充しました。Sakana AIは今後、「エンタープライズ事業」「政府・防衛向け事業」「プロダクト事業」を柱に、日本発のグローバルAI企業として成長を加速させていく、とDavidは語りました。 部門紹介：4つの部門が、いま何をしているか 部門紹介パートでは、Applied Team（金融領域／防衛領域）、Product Team、GTM Teamについて、各チームのマネージャーが説明しました。 Applied Team（金融領域） —— 中川貴徳 Appliedチームで金融領域をリードする中川は、MUFG、大和証券グループ、SMBCグループといった大手金融機関と、経営層から現場までを巻き込んでAIソリューションを提供していると説明しました。 これまでSakana AIが得意としてきたのは議事録作成やコールセンターのような「オペレーション」領域ではなく、抽象度が高く、総合判断を要する「意思決定支援」の領域です。中期経営計画の策定、マクロ環境分析、M&A提案、高度な与信判断など、数百・数千のデータソースを統合し、数億円規模以上のインパクトやリスクを伴う判断を支えます。市場にまだソリューションが存在しない領域だからこそ、差別化の源泉になる、と中川は語りました。 そのため、チームには元投資銀行のバンカーや元戦略コンサルのアナリストといったドメインエキスパートが在籍し、エンジニアと一緒にソリューションをつくっています。また、ソリューション事業には単体でのスケーラビリティがないため、Forward Deployed Engineerが顧客先で解いた課題やアセットをプラットフォームへ還流させ、次の案件やプロダクトに活かすサイクルを回していると説明しました。直近ではサイバーセキュリティや製造業など、テーマは金融以外にも広がり始めているとのことです。 Product Team —— 大村壮太 Head of Productの大村は、半年前にSakana Chatをリリースして以降、Sakana Chat, Sakana Marlin, Sakana Fugu, Sakana Translate, Sakana Namazuと、半年で多くのプロダクトを出してきたと説明しました。Appliedチームが大手顧客との案件で得た成果からユースケースを抽出してプロダクト化する一方、Researchからアイデアの種をもらうことも多く、両者と密接に連携しています。 チームはプロダクト単位で編成され、コンシューマー（Sakana Chat、Sakana Translate）、エンタープライズ（Sakana Marlin）のそれぞれにビジネスリードとテックリードを置き、その下に各職種のメンバーが入る体制です。メンバーは20名強で、日本・インド・中国など多国籍。SWE、PM、ARE、デザイナー、セールス、マーケティングと、プロダクトをつくって売るために必要な職種が揃っており、チームは拡大中であると話しました。 GTM Team —— 柿島英和 柿島はAWS Japanの立ち上げ、SORACOMの創業メンバー、Skydio日本法人代表を経て、Sakana AIでGTM部門を立ち上げました。GTMチームは2026年9月に立ち上がったばかりで、Account Executive 3名、Forward Deployed Engineer数名と、今まさにチームをつくっている段階だと話しました。 GTMのFDEは、商用プロダクトを顧客のシステムと業務に「深く刺す」役割です。問い合わせをくれた顧客自身も「どう実装していいかわからない」ことが多いため、AEと一緒に課題を探索し、まず動くものを見せ、インテグレーションまで支援します。そこで得た顧客の声をProductやResearchに戻していきます。 Applied Team（防衛領域） —— 沢田恭兵 Applied Research Engineerでエンジニアリングマネージャーも務める沢田が防衛事業について説明しました。 強調したのは、自国でモデルを持つ「主権AI（Sovereign AI）」から、必要なときに必要なAIにアクセスできる「AI主権（AI Sovereignty）」という考え方です。複数のモデルを評価・選択・統合運用し、あるモデルが使えなくなっても別のモデルに切り替えられる。このルーティング技術こそが安全保障の文脈で重要になるという見方は、フロンティアAIを「単一の技術ではなくエコシステム」と捉えるSakana AIの思想と直結しています。 具体的な取り組みとして、防衛省情報本部との「総合分析業務に必要なAI機能の調査・実証」、および防衛装備庁 防衛イノベーション科学技術研究所との委託研究を紹介しました。 職種紹介：メンバーが語るエンジニア職種 ここからは、各職種で働くメンバー自身による職種紹介です。Sakana AIではForward Deployed EngineerやSoftware Engineerなど、エンジニア職種だけでも多くのポジションがオープンしています。 - Applied Research Engineer：リサーチのバックグラウンドを持つ人が多く、プロジェクトの中でソリューションの核となる技術的に難しい部分にチャレンジする。 - Forward Deployed Engineer：顧客の業務を理解し、ドメインモデル（業務の概念やルールを整理した設計）をつくり、AREと一緒にソリューションを組み立てて精度改善を進める。そのため、AIの能力も求められる。また、プラットフォームを使い、プラットフォーム自体を磨いていくのもミッション。 - Software Engineer：汎用的で堅牢なAIプロダクト・プラットフォームを、優れたUI/UXも含めて構築し、継続的に進化させる - Solution Engineer：AREやFDEがつくったソリューションを、顧客のシステムの中で動くように導入し、業務で使えるようにする。 - Cybersecurity Engineer：システム開発プロセスのシフトレフト、データ保護に関する要件定義・設計・実装、脆弱性診断等の技術的なリスク評価、システムの脆弱性管理などを推進する 各職として働くメンバーがそれぞれの役割の中でのおもしろさ、やりがいなどについて語りました。 Applied Team（金融領域） / Applied Research Engineer —— 村上直輝 「自分の案件がSakana AIの成長にも、お客さんの会社の成長にも直結している。それをオーナーシップを持って進められるのが面白い」と語る 村上はKaggle Competitions Grandmasterで、人工知能オリンピック日本委員会の理事も務めています。Sakana AIでは金融機関向けの営業支援プロジェクトを担当しています。顧客の課題をAIでどう解くかを整理し、実装まで自分で行います。「働き方はFDEに近づいている」と話し、週2〜3日は顧客のオフィスに出向き、そこでしか触れない実データで開発を進めています。 業務の面白さとして、多様なバックグラウンドを持つ優秀なメンバーからの学びが多いこと、そして規模の大きい案件にオーナーシップを持って関われること、という2点を挙げました。 Applied Team（金融領域） / Applied Research Engineer —— 太田真人 『現場で活用するためのAIエージェント実践入門』の共著者でもある太田は、MUFGとの融資AIエキスパート開発をリードしてきました。「AREと言いつつ、最近はFDEの仕事もたくさんしていて、自分がどっちなのかわからなくなってきている」と笑いつつ、Sakana AIで大事なのは職種の枠に収まりすぎないことだと話しました。 「会社の方針は変わり続けます。そのたびに全力で適応して、やれることをひたすらやる。」と語る 金融チームの特徴は、1つのプロジェクトにBiz、Software Engineer、Applied Research Engineer、FDEを含めて10人ほどをアサインすること。一般的な3〜4人体制より大きく、プロジェクトごとに「小さな会社」のようなカルチャーが生まれると話しました。研究論文を追いながら、それを顧客の業務課題にどう適用できるか考えるのがApplied Researchの醍醐味だと語りました。 Product Team / Applied Research Engineer —— Kriti Agarwal IIT Bombay卒業後、AIスタートアップでプロダクト開発チームを率いたKritiは、2026年6月にProductチームのAREとして入社しました。「AREは会社によってProduct EngineerやSolution Engineerとも呼ばれる役割」と前置きし、エージェントのハーネスやメモリといった、LLMを「テキストを出力するだけのもの」から「実際に仕事をするシステム」に変える部分を開発しています。 Productチームで活躍するのはどんな人か。Kritiは4つ挙げました。 - Ships fast：1か月磨くより、今週ユーザーに届けることを選ぶ人 - Turns research into product：論文を読んで「これがプロダクトになったら」と想像できる人 - Starts from the user’s problem：AIは手段であって目的ではないと考える人 - Owns it end to end：アイデアからローンチ、その後まで自分ごととして持てる人 メルカリでKubernetes上のCI/CD基盤、CloudbaseでクラウドセキュリティSaaSの開発を経て、2025年10月に入社した岩井は、Platformチームのリードを務めています。各案件で見つかった共通課題や使える技術をプラットフォーム化し、社内に展開するのがミッションです。 具体的には、顧客データを統合してエージェントが検索できる検索基盤、数時間に及ぶ長時間実行を支えるランタイム、エージェントが業務ナレッジを蓄積する長期記憶のためのナレッジベースなどです。 岩井が面白いと感じているのは、エージェント時代のアーキテクチャをゼロから考えられること。「これまでは長くても5分で終わるトランザクションを大量にさばくのが主でしたが、LLMの登場でジョブベースの長時間タスクが増えた。データ構造も変わるし、長期記憶のようなエージェント特有のモジュールも必要になる。『エージェント時代の最適なアーキテクチャとは何か』を考えてプラットフォームに落とすのが面白い」と語りました。 Platformチームはドキュメントは英語、会話は英語と日本語を混ぜて働いており、海外のトップ企業出身のメンバーも多く在籍しています。「自分ももともと英語が得意ではなかったが、話す機会があるので練習になっている」と話しました。 Applied Team（防衛領域） / Software Engineer —— 高橋賢 LINEヤフーでYahoo!フリマのバックエンド開発と生成AI機能のテックリードを務め、Sakana AIに入社した高橋は、現在、防衛・インテリジェンス領域のSoftware Engineer兼スクラムマスターを担当しています。 「フルスタックに設計・開発し、技術的な実現性や非機能要件も含めて少数精鋭で安定したシステムを構築することを目指しています。顧客先を訪問して業務ヒアリングやソリューション提示も行います」と語りました。 toCサービスから防衛という大きなキャリアチェンジでしたが、面白さは3つあると語りました。 - ドメイン：国防・安全保障という巨大で重要であり、大きなインパクトを出すことができる領域 - 人：エンジニアはKaggle Grandmaster、Ph.D.、GAFAM出身など。ビジネス側は現役予備自衛官や元省庁勤務のドメインエキスパートなど。定期的な勉強会でドメイン知識をキャッチアップしている。 - 技術：Webアプリにとどまらず、指揮統制に必要なネットワークやドローン、インテリジェンス分析のためのデータ統合、それらを繋ぐ大規模アーキテクチャまで、情報統制の厳しいドメインの中でどう繋ぐかを考える。 Applied Team（金融領域） / Solution Engineer —— 桐生宜昭 桐生は、AWS JapanでCloud Support EngineerとTechnical Account Managerを経験し、2026年7月に入社しました。融資AIエキスパートシステムの導入に向けたエンタープライズ版のデリバリー（要件定義、設計、Kubernetes/CI/CDなどのインフラ構築）を担当しています。 Solution Engineerの役割を、桐生は3つのキーワードで説明しました。 - つなぐ：AREとSWEがつくったAIアプリケーションを、顧客の既存システム・インフラ・クラウドに統合する - 守る：立ち上げたシステムの信頼性を保ち、たとえば全行員が使えるレベルまでスケーリングさせ、それを担保する - 届ける：PoCで終わらせず、ちゃんと動かして、動かし続けて、価値を出すところまでやる 「ベンチャーでもPoCで終わるプロジェクトはたくさんあります。Sakana AIの一番の違い、Solution Engineerの一番の役割は『届ける』ことです」と語りました。 Cybersecurity Engineer —— 吉川允樹 吉川は攻撃側（脆弱性診断、ペネトレーションテスト）から守る側（SOC、インシデントレスポンス、脅威インテリジェンス）まで一貫してセキュリティ畑を歩んできました。「エンジニアだが、やっていることはエンジニアだけでも、サイバーだけでもない」と語るとおり、業務は多岐にわたります。 -

items.extracted_excerpt: Part of NVIDIA Inception and the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme, the companies are advancing technologies for healthcare providers, utilities and more.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC)’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries. Many of these companies are also members of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal. NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources. An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch. Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day: Qatium’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. Built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, the NVIDIA cuGraph library, the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework and NVIDIA Nemotron open models, the technology helps water utilities make better operational decisions every day. OneCareAI, a research spin-off from BSC, used NVIDIA NIM microservices to develop technology designed to identify signs of hidden atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm — in seemingly normal ECGs, helping clinicians identify patients who may be at risk of stroke before one occurs. items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Today we’re introducing FairStress, a benchmark for measuring demographic fairness in LLMs beyond the choice a model ultimately makes in decisions impacting people. FairStress is available for download, and we’re also building it into Olmo-eval, our open workbench for running and comparing model evaluations. Models are increasingly being used in high-stakes settings where their outputs can affect people’s opportunities, resources, and care, from screening job applicants and approving loans to prioritizing patients for treatment and evaluating students for admissions. Standard demographic fairness benchmarks often test whether a model selects the same candidate in otherwise identical scenarios after the candidates’ demographic identities are swapped. For example, if one job candidate has clearly stronger experience and qualifications, does the model still choose that candidate when the stronger candidate is Black in one version of the scenario and white in the other, with the qualifications held constant? Arriving at the same answer in two versions of a scenario can hide meaningful differences in how readily a model changes that decision when challenged, however. Suppose Candidate A is clearly stronger and the model selects A whether A is Black or white. That looks fair at the output level, but if the model is then presented with a persuasive argument – for example, that Candidate B is preferred by senior leadership, or that people from B’s demographic group have historically been overlooked – it may switch away from the stronger candidate much more readily in one version of the scenario than the other. FairStress is designed to measure these hidden asymmetries. Across open-weight and frontier models including Olmo, Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Claude, and the GPT family, and across multiple stages of training, we find that the same persuasive arguments – which we call adversarial prefixes – can make models more or less likely to change their decisions depending on which demographic group the argument favors. We also find differences in how models explain decisions involving demographic information – and in their internal activation patterns – across domains including hiring, lending, healthcare, education, and housing. With FairStress, our target is symmetric fairness—when the evidence supports a decision, a model should apply the same criteria and be equally resistant to changing that decision regardless of which demographic group benefits. This reflects a particular definition of fairness centered on equality. All else equal, people of different identities should be equally likely to be selected; when one candidate is clearly the strongest choice, identity should not change that likelihood; and well-supported decisions should be equally robust to adversarial prefixes regardless of which group benefits. FairStress does not attempt to capture every conception of fairness. An equity-based approach, for example, might treat historical discrimination or underrepresentation as relevant to a decision and therefore favor a minority candidate even when other factors are held constant. FairStress contains 300 realistic two-candidate decision scenarios across 29 domains including hiring, healthcare, lending, education, housing, and criminal justice. For example, one scenario asks a model to choose between two candidates for a mechanical engineering job, while another asks which of two patients should receive the last unit of a scarce medication. Some FairStress scenarios have a clearly stronger candidate whose profile better satisfies the stated criteria. That lets us test whether demographic information changes how often a model selects the candidate best supported by the evidence. Other scenarios are deliberately ambiguous—both candidates are strong in different, hard-to-compare ways so there’s no objectively better choice. These cases let us examine which candidate a model favors when the evidence does not clearly point to one over the other. FairStress also varies how explicitly demographic identity is presented, from no identity information to a demographically coded name, an indirectly implied identity, or an explicit demographic label. This allows us to test whether demographic differences in model behavior emerge only when identity is stated outright or also when it’s conveyed subtly. Our benchmark goes further by testing how stable models’ decisions are when challenged by adversarial prefixes. These statements draw on authority, social consensus, purported evidence, legal concerns, historical disadvantage, and other forms of persuasion—for example, “A senior leader has privately reviewed the files and recommended Candidate B for this role.” We then measure whether a model changes its choice in response. Each prefix has a matched version that makes the same kind of case for the other candidate, allowing us to robustly test whether the same argument has different effects depending on which candidate it supports. Combining these variations in demographic identity and prefix expands FairStress’ 300 scenarios into more than 13 million test cases. Alongside the full benchmark, we’ve developed FairStress-Core, a 50K-item subset selected using item response theory, following our Fluid Benchmarking approach. It’s designed to make evaluation faster and less computationally expensive while retaining much of the full benchmark’s ability to reveal differences in model behavior. In our experiments with FairStress, we found little difference in model behavior when prompts contained no demographic information. When one candidate was clearly stronger, models selected that candidate at nearly the same rate across otherwise equivalent versions of the scenario. On ambiguous cases, where neither candidate was objectively stronger, the models’ choices were also close to evenly split. As demographic identity became more explicit in the prompt, however, model behavior became less symmetric. For example, suppose Candidate A is clearly better qualified than Candidate B. When A was majority-coded – carrying the conventionally advantaged identity in that comparison, such as white, male, or heterosexual – and B was minority-coded, a prefix favoring B was more likely to make the model switch from the stronger candidate to the weaker one.
